questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The outer faces of a triptych
questions.learningObjective: State the purpose of the outer faces of a triptych
questions.stem: A clerk logging the panels of a triptych notes that the outside of the two wings carries a pattern unrelated to the interior scenes. What are the outer faces of a triptych for?

options.text: To close the altarpiece, so the shut work presents its own coherent outward image
To record the donor and the date, so the outer faces act as a legal document
options.misconception: mistakes the outer wings for a record of ownership

options.text: To prove the wings were repainted, since the outer paint differs from the inner
options.misconception: reads a difference in paint as evidence of repainting

options.text: To copy the interior scenes in reverse, so the outer faces show the same story
options.misconception: believes the outer faces simply repeat the interior

questions.explanation: The outer faces are painted as a proper image in their own right, because a closed altarpiece is still seen. Reading them as documents, as proof of repainting or as a copy of the interior misses what they are.
questions.hint: Think about what a visitor sees when the wings are shut.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A band of secco loss on a fresco wall
questions.learningObjective: Explain how secco loss differs from a loss in buon fresco
questions.stem: A deposition witness described the band of lost paint along the foot of the wall. Write one sentence explaining why a band of secco loss differs from a loss in the buon fresco beneath it.

answer.exemplar: A band of secco loss is confined to the coat painted onto dry plaster, so the lime plaster beneath it survives and still holds the picture's incisions and its day's work, whereas a loss in the buon fresco takes the plaster itself with them; the two kinds of damage therefore have different shapes and different remedies.

questions.explanation: Secco sits on top of the plaster, so losing it leaves the wall and its incisions intact. Treating the loss as a structural break through the plaster, or as a modern scrape, misidentifies the damage.
questions.hint: Ask what layer the secco was applied to.

answer.exemplar: A band of secco loss removes only the coat painted onto the dry plaster, so the wall beneath, with its incisions and the edges of its day's work, is still there and can be matched back in; a loss of plaster takes the wall's fabric itself, which is a different and far more serious structural problem.

options.text: That the wood was too green when the panel was made, and no coating could have helped

options.text: That the panel should have been larger, so the movement would have been less
options.misconception: invents a design remedy for a preparation fault

options.text: That the coating has to be well keyed to the timber, or paint and ground move apart with it

questions.explanation: A crack that follows the movement of the wood shows the ground and paint must be well keyed to the timber. Blaming the timber's age, the panel's size or an unfinished state puts the fault in the wrong place.
questions.hint: Ask what has to hold the layers together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a ground gives the painter to work on
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how a ground shows through thin paint
questions.stem: The schedule lists the shutters as having a warm pinkish grey ground, and the sky passages above them are painted thinly so the ground shows through. Twenty of thirty viewers said the skies looked warm rather than white. Which reading fits?

options.text: The sky is simply painted in a warm colour, and the ground has nothing to do with it
options.misconception: denies the visible effect of the ground

options.text: The ground is working inside the picture, warming the thin passages above it
The panel was varnished too warmly, so the skies are discoloured
options.misconception: attributes the warmth to varnish rather than to paint and ground

options.text: Most visitors mis-saw the skies, since white skies are the usual convention
options.misconception: dismisses a consistent reading as error

questions.explanation: The ground warms the thin sky passages, and most viewers read them as warm, so the layer is working inside the picture. Denying the effect, blaming varnish or dismissing the readings as error misuses the notices.
questions.hint: Twenty of thirty read the skies as warm.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The outer faces of a triptych
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the outer faces of a triptych are for
questions.stem: A conservator's note records that the outer faces have lost more colour than the interior panels. Write one sentence explaining what the outer faces of a triptych are for.

answer.exemplar: The outer faces are the public face of the altarpiece, and because a triptych is closed for most of its working life they were given their own designed images, so that the shut object presents a picture of equal dignity; their greater loss simply reflects that they stood exposed to handling, dust and weather.

questions.explanation: The outer faces exist to make the closed altarpiece a finished image in its own right. Reading their extra loss as poor workmanship or as evidence that they were never meant to be seen contradicts the design.
questions.hint: Think about how the work is most often seen.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A predella read as a sequence
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the difference in width between two predella panels
questions.stem: The predella's five panels are numbered in reading order. The second panel is 0.72 m wide and the third is 0.84 m wide. How many centimetres wider is the third panel than the second?
questions.explanation: The third panel exceeds the second by 0.84 - 0.72 = 0.12 m, that is 12 cm. Adding the two widths would give a total rather than the difference asked for.
questions.hint: Subtract the narrower from the wider.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A band of secco loss on a fresco wall
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish two bands of loss by the survey evidence

stimulus.body: The survey of the north wall records a horizontal strip 0.30 m high where the colour layer is gone, running unbroken from the dado to the corner. Along the strip the plaster is rough and light, and the pits of the underlying intonaco are visible. Where the fresco above was painted wet, the same area shows plaster with the colours still bonded into it.

questions.stem: What does the wall survey show about the two bands of loss on the north wall?

options.text: Both bands are plaster losses, since both show bare plaster
options.misconception: ignores the difference the survey records

options.text: Both bands are secco losses, since they run at the same height
options.misconception: assumes one height means one technique

options.text: The lower band is a secco loss, and the upper band takes plaster and colour together
The upper band is a secco loss, since the plaster beneath it survives intact
options.misconception: reverses which band lost its plaster

questions.explanation: The lower strip shows bare plaster with the intonaco pits, while the wet-painted band above has lost plaster and colour together, so the two are different failures. Assuming one technique for both reverses the evidence.
questions.hint: Look at what survives in each band.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mirror that includes the viewer
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a mirror does and why a blank face suits it
questions.stem: The final entry in the file notes that the reflected figure in the mirror has no face. First say what the mirror does for the picture; then say why leaving the face blank is consistent with that purpose.

options.text: It hides the panel's damage, and the blank face conceals a repair
options.misconception: turns the blank into evidence of damage

options.text: It enlarges the room, and the blank face shows the painter had no model available
options.misconception: explains the blankness by a practical shortage

options.text: It repeats the main figure, and the blank face shows the copy was unfinished
options.misconception: reads the blank as incomplete work

options.text: It places the viewer inside the scene, and a blank face lets whoever stands there become the face

questions.explanation: A mirror that includes the viewer lets whoever stands there occupy the reflected place, so a blank face lets the viewer supply it. Reading the blank as a shortage, unfinished work or concealed damage misses the purpose.
questions.hint: Ask who would occupy the blank face.
